# Esther 2: Research Notes, Verse by Verse

**A note on sources:** I fetched the full Enduring Word (Guzik) and Pulpit Commentary pages, so points from those two are summarised with their URLs and have no citation tags. Everything else comes from search-result extracts.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says "after these things" covers more than chapter 1. Comparing with 2:16, he puts four years between the chapters. In that time Xerxes invaded Greece, failed, and came home defeated, looking for sensual distractions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks the king remembered Vashti with regret, and may have begun to wonder whether her punishment was too harsh. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Precept Austin lists three things the king remembered: Vashti (her beauty), Vashti's refusal to obey and his decree against her banishing her from his presence, a decree which was irreversible. https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_1-2_commentary
- Ellicott dates the marriage after the return from Greece, which explains the delay. He adds that even in this gap the king was entangled in more than one illicit connection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/2.htm

**vv. 2–4**
- Pulpit: the courtiers had brought about Vashti's fall, so they feared that if she came back they would be dismissed or executed. That is why they offered a new plan. It also comments sharply on the "purification": the king was treated as so divine that even pure young women had to be purified before meeting him, though he himself was far from pure. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Pulpit's sermon notes: the advice was bad in itself, for the king, for the young women and for their families, but providence overruled it for good. It warns that this gives no licence to "do evil that good may come." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Guzik calls it a kind of "Miss Persian Empire" contest. He cites Josephus that 400 women were chosen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- Precept Austin: the Hebrew word for "virgin" (*bethulah*) means marriage aged maidens, not necessarily virgins in the sense that they had never had sexual relations. Quoting Ferguson, it notes the irony: after the king said Vashti's place should go to someone better, the only requirement for a new Queen was beauty, youth, and virginity. It also points out that repeatedly we see the king taking the advice of others. https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_1-2_commentary
- On v. 3, Pulpit explains the "house of the women" as a separate building with several parts. Hegai seems to have been keeper of the virgins in particular. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: after a story set entirely in the Persian court, a Jew suddenly appears. The family line connects the book to the rest of Scripture. The name Mordecai is almost certainly linked to the Babylonian god Marduk, though it may have been given without any thought of its meaning. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Firth (Gospel Coalition): His status as a Jew is stressed by the Hebrew word order before a genealogy is provided. The key point is that it echoes Saul's genealogy (1Sam 9:1), even if the significance of this only emerges later. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/esther/
- Ellicott thinks the names are probably Mordecai's actual father, grandfather and great-grandfather. Others take them as famous ancestors (Shimei who cursed David, Kish the father of Saul). Ellicott is critical of Mordecai: an ambitious, worldly man; who, though numbers of his tribe had returned to the land of their fathers, preferred to remain behind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/2.htm

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: "who was carried away" most naturally refers to Kish, not Mordecai. If it meant Mordecai, the king could not be Xerxes. Kish went in the second deportation, under Jeconiah, in 597 BC. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Firth agrees. The awkward Hebrew is best understood as suggesting that his ancestor Kish had been among those exiled by Nebuchadnezzar a century earlier. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/esther/
- Catholic.com: Mordecai was born when his parents were already in captivity, which was why he was given a Babylonian name, derived from the name of the god Marduk. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/judith-and-esther

**v. 7**
- Guzik: Hadassah means "myrtle" and Esther means "star." He quotes Baldwin that in prophecy the myrtle stands for the Lord's forgiveness and acceptance of his people (Isaiah 41:19; 55:13). The family belonged to the exiles who chose not to go back to Judah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- Pulpit: "Esther" may come from Ishtar ("Venus") or from a Persian word for "star." She was Mordecai's first cousin, probably much younger. He may not have formally adopted her, but he raised her as his own child. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Gill (labelled Baptist and Calvinist on the site) mentions a Targum view that "Esther" comes from *satar*, "to hide." He prefers the Persian meaning "star." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/2-7.html
- Pulpit's sermon notes treat Mordecai's adoption of Esther as a picture of God adopting believers. Matthew Henry points to God as *Father of the fatherless.* https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_002.cfm

**v. 8**
- Guzik: It seems that Esther didn't really have a choice about this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- Firth: There is no indication that Esther sought this. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/esther/
- Pulpit takes a different line. The Hebrew word does not imply force, and Persian Jews probably saw it as an honour. It mentions a Targum story that Mordecai hid Esther until the king's authority forced him to give her up. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Commentators disagree about whether Mordecai put her forward. Don Smith says there is little evidence to support the idea that Mordecai placed his daughter into the pageant. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_don/Esther/Esther-TheStudyofProvidence/Esther_02.cfm Deffinbaugh (bible.org), by contrast, says Mordecai is the one who seems to enter her in the contest for queen. https://bible.org/seriespage/hanging-out-gate-esther-219-315

**v. 9**
- Guzik: Esther's favour with Hegai fulfils Proverbs 3:3–4. The Hebrew for "beauty preparations" comes from a root meaning "to scour, to polish." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- Pulpit: "obtained favour" is a favourite phrase of this book's author. Her "portions" probably means her daily food. Each young woman seems to have had seven attendants. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Utley (bible.org) notes that apparently Esther ate the king's food (unlike Daniel). She may not have known the food laws, or she was hiding who she was. https://bible.org/seriespage/esther-2
- Ferguson, quoted at Precept Austin, says Scripture forbade marrying a pagan, sex outside marriage and unclean food, and Esther did all three. https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_1-2_commentary

**v. 10** (the most debated verse in the chapter)
- **Approving views:**
  - Pulpit: telling people she was Jewish would probably have caused prejudice against her. She was not guilty of falsehood, or of deceit, in acting as she did. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
  - Bible Hub's study notes call it strategic discretion, comparing Joseph and Moses: Esther never repudiates Yahweh; she merely withholds ethnicity. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_hide_Jewish_identity_Esther_2_10.htm
- **A middle view:** Guzik says Christians normally have no good reason to hide their faith (Matthew 10:32–33). But God may sometimes direct reticence, not for the purposes of permanently concealing it, but waiting for the opportune moment to reveal it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- **Critical views:**
  - Ligonier (Reformed) says Esther and Mordecai were not perfect saints. Unlike Daniel, they cared little to be known as God's holy people. It notes the author does not give their motives. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/such-time
  - Constable's notes quote a writer who argues that if they kept the food laws, their true nationality would have quickly been discovered. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/2-7.html
  - Deffinbaugh accuses Mordecai of a double standard: he refused to bow (chapter 3) yet made Esther hide her identity, so Esther must have bowed to her king and to his officials. https://bible.org/seriespage/hanging-out-gate-esther-219-315

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: Mordecai seems to have been one of the porters at the palace gate, and visited the court in front of the harem each day for news. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Utley reads the daily visits as a sign of his love for his adopted daughter and of his fear of anti-Semitism. https://bible.org/seriespage/esther-2
- Matthew Henry holds him up as an example of care for relatives whom providence has placed in our charge. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_002.cfm

**v. 12**
- Guzik describes Persian bridal customs. One suggested reason for the twelve months was to make sure no woman was already pregnant. He quotes Matthew Poole's blunt remark about body odour in hot countries. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- Pulpit: myrrh was prized for its scent and purifying power. It was used in Israel's holy anointing oil (Exodus 30). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: when each woman left for the king's rooms, she could ask for any dress or ornament she liked, and it had to be given to her. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: the women's quarters had at least three houses: the queen's, the concubines' (the "second house") and the virgins'. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- GotQuestions: The fact that each woman spent the night with the king implies sexual relations. As for Esther's choice, Her choice was likely either submit or die. https://www.gotquestions.org/Esther-Xerxes.html
- Guzik: the women who were not chosen stayed in the harem, could never marry, and lived like permanent widows. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- Precept Austin: This is no heart-warming romantic Cinderella or Beauty and the Beast story. https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_1-2_commentary

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: Esther did not rely on outward ornament and left everything to Hegai. "Found favour" may describe her life in general or that particular evening. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Guzik: following Hegai's advice showed humble wisdom. Her favour came from both her godliness and her beauty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- Don Smith: Hegai gave her inside advice about what the king liked. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_don/Esther/Esther-TheStudyofProvidence/Esther_02.cfm

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: this is the only mention of the month Tebeth in Scripture (late December to early January). It falls four years after Vashti's fall, probably January 479 BC, just after Xerxes came back defeated from Greece. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Precept Austin gives 478BC. https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_1-2_commentary

**v. 17**
- Guzik: this was no accident but God's plan (Psalm 75:6–7). God can use human evil without causing it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- Ellicott: a second gathering of virgins (v. 19) took place within five years, which shows how the word "love "is degraded in this connection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/2.htm
- Pulpit's sermon notes: providence raised the crown and also raised the humble head to receive it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: the "release" was a break from taxes, military service, or both, for a set period. Persian kings were known for giving gifts. The name "Esther's feast" suggests the event was long remembered. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Firth: the king does what he so often does, hosting another feast. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/esther/

**v. 19**
- Precept Austin: the "second gathering" Meaning is uncertain. The city gate was where trade and legal business took place, which suggests Mordecai held some official position. https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_1-2_commentary
- Guzik: sitting in the gate linked Mordecai with the decision-makers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/

**v. 20**
- Clarke: the Septuagint (Greek Old Testament) adds here that Mordecai told Esther to fear God and keep his commandments. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/2-23.html
- Guzik discusses why God's name is missing from the book: the drinking at Purim, possible hidden acrostics of YHWH, or Persian censorship. His preferred answer is that the book shows God working behind the scenes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- A sermon by D. Rowlands, printed in the Pulpit Commentary, rejects excusing their choices on the ground that they were carrying out the designs of Providence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-2.html
- Coffman: keeping the secret was vital to what happened. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/2-23.html

**vv. 21–22**
- Guzik: Mordecai did not think, "I'm an exile, so why should I care if the pagan king dies." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-2/
- Matthew Henry: an example for good subjects not to conceal any bad design they know of against the prince or the public peace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/2-23.html
- Deffinbaugh: saving the king may not have even been from kind intentions toward the king. Mordecai may have been protecting Esther's position. https://bible.org/seriespage/hanging-out-gate-esther-219-315
- Ellicott: reporting the plot gave Esther more influence with the king, which helped her later. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/2.htm

**v. 23**
- **"Gallows" is literally "tree."** Most writers think this means impalement on a stake rather than hanging with a rope: Guzik, Ellicott ("crucified"), Barnes, Pulpit and Constable. Gill is the exception: Josephus says they were crucified; but hanging was frequent among the Persians, as Grotius observes, and better agrees with the word here used. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/2-23.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/2-23.htm
- The Cambridge Bible notes the Septuagint says the king "examined" the two men, which probably means by torture. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/2-23.htm
- On the royal record book: Ellicott connects it to the king's sleepless night in chapter 6. Matthew Henry says of Mordecai, He was not rewarded presently, but a book of remembrance was written. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/2.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/2-21.html

---

## Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no disagreement on this chapter that runs along denominational lines. I found nothing from Lutheran, Methodist or Pentecostal teachers specifically on Esther 2, apart from Guzik on Enduring Word, the site you list as Pentecostal and charismatic. What I did find is agreement across traditions on providence and a split over how good Esther and Mordecai were:
- **On providence, all agree.** Ligonier (Reformed) says leaving out God's name is the author's way of depicting the hidden hand of providence https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/esther. Spurgeon (Baptist, quoted at Precept Austin) saw in Esther a wonderful instance of His providence https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_1-2_commentary.
- **On the characters, they split.** The positive readings come from Pulpit, Guzik and Bible Hub. The critical readings come from Ligonier, Ellicott, Deffinbaugh and Ferguson (see v. 10 and v. 5 above).

## Other views

- **Modern scholarship:** Bible Odyssey says the debate over Esther's character comes from her secrecy. Some interpreters feared that Esther had assimilated to the ways of the Gentile palace. Partly for this reason the book's place in the canon was uncertain for centuries. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/esther/ I found no NET Bible notes on this chapter.
- **The Greek additions:** The Wesley Center says the additions introduce references to God (50 times) and Jewish religion, probably to make up for what the Hebrew text lacks. https://wesley.nnu.edu/sermons-essays-books/noncanonical-literature/noncanonical-literature-ot-apocrypha/additions-to-esther/ One addition has Esther's prayer excusing her marriage to the uncircumcised king. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/mse/e/esther-apocryphal-additions-to-the-book-of.html
- **Catholic:** The Catholic canon includes the additions. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/esther/ Haydock calls the Greek and Hebrew versions equally inspired. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/esther.html Catholic.com says the liturgy prefers the Greek text because it states openly what the Hebrew only hints at. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/judith-and-esther
- **Early church (Syriac):** Aphrahat reads Esther as a type of the Church. Esther pleased the king and replaced Vashti, just as the Church pleases God and has replaced the congregation which did not His Will. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/370121.htm
- **Prosperity, word of faith and hyper-grace teaching:** I found nothing on these sites about such readings of Esther 2.
